items.summary: We give an explicit convex polygon with 63 rational vertices whose area, after its shortest closed Euclidean billiard length is normalized to one, is smaller than that of Mallée’s parabolic triangle. This disproves Conjecture 2.2 of Balitskiy, Mitrofanov and Polyanskii (2026). The polygon was found by moving supporting lines near the parabolic triangle’s focal contacts and then discretizing the resulting shape. The proof checks the literal polygon in exact rational arithmetic: 63 width directions and all 39,711 triples of supporting edge lines. A three-file verification package contains the coordinates and an independent checker. The result identifies a better competitor, without claiming that it is optimal.
items.title: A rational polygonal counterexample to the Mallée parabolic triangle conjecture

items.summary: This chapter develops the research programme of Generative Relational Economics (GRE) by translating the conceptual, methodological, and substantive architectures developed earlier in the book into a cumulative, contestable, and revisable programme of inquiry. Its principal concern is answerability: GRE claims should specify what is being investigated, what kinds of evidence can support them, what would count against them, which methods are appropriate to their objects, and under what conditions their scope, formulation, or status should change. The chapter first distinguishes the epistemic status of GRE claims and establishes a modular research architecture. It then formulates research programmes for relational economic structures, allocation, heterogeneous value, value conversion and circulation, generative return, generative spacetime, fast–slow dynamics, economic power, justice, generative exploitation, epistemic economy, and AI-mediated capability asymmetry. These substantive programmes are complemented by domain studies, formal modelling, historical and interpretive inquiry, quantitative and empirical research, comparative theory, institutional experimentation, measurement analysis, counterevidence, negative results, replication, reinterpretation, and research infrastructure. A recurring concern is to prevent operationalization from collapsing the distinctions that motivate GRE. Measurement is therefore treated as a transformation with possible loss and reflexive effects; formalization is treated as task-relative rather than as evidence of ontological commitment; justice research keeps normative premises explicit; power and exploitation require mechanism-level identification rather than inference from asymmetry alone; and cross-domain translation preserves non-equivalence and domain-specific remainders. Failed models, failed translations, null results, counterexamples, and negative evidence are treated as constitutive resources for cumulative research rather than as residuals to be discarded. The chapter concludes by specifying how GRE may interact with neighboring Generative Relational domains while retaining disciplinary containment. Candidate cross-domain structures remain hypotheses for further inquiry rather than presumptive components of a completed general theory. GRE thereby emerges not as a closed theoretical system, but as an open research programme whose concepts, methods, models, and domain claims remain historically situated, empirically answerable, formally inspectable, and institutionally revisable.

items.summary: It is an open problem in proof complexity whether every unsatisfiable CNF formula has an FPT-sized resolution refutation parameterized by incidence treewidth. In this paper, we establish several upper bounds on resolution refutation length related to this problem. Consider an unsatisfiable CNF formula $F$ with $n$ variables, $m$ clauses, maximum clause width $k$, and incidence treewidth $\mathrm{tw}^*(F)$. In this paper, we introduce two variants of incidence treewidth. Their definitions can be stated informally as follows. The first is log-weighted incidence treewidth $\mathrm{tw}_{\log}^*(F)$, which is the treewidth of the weighted incidence graph, in which variables have weight one and each clause has weight equal to the logarithm of its width. The second is partially log-weighted incidence treewidth $\mathrm{tw}^*_{\mathrm{plog}}(F)$, which is a refinement of log-weighted incidence treewidth. In this variant, for a nice tree decomposition of the incidence graph, each clause has weight one along a path selected for that clause and elsewhere has weight equal to the logarithm of one plus the number of its literals whose variables do not appear in any bag on that path, and variables have weight one. For every unsatisfiable CNF formula $F$, we prove the existence of (i) an FPT-sized resolution refutation parameterized by log-weighted incidence treewidth, with width at most $\mathrm{tw}_{\log}^*(F)+k$; (ii) a resolution refutation of length $(n+m)k^{O(\mathrm{tw}^*(F))}$ and width at most $\mathrm{tw}^*(F)+k$; (iii) an FPT-sized resolution refutation parameterized by partially log-weighted incidence treewidth; and (iv) an FPT-sized regular resolution refutation parameterized by log-weighted incidence treewidth. Our main idea is to construct FPT-sized $k$-DNF resolution refutations parameterized by incidence treewidth, and then convert them into resolution refutations.
items.title: Short Resolution Refutations for CNFs with Bounded Weighted Incidence Treewidth

items.summary: We present a complete, self-contained analysis of the one-loop functional renormalization group (FRG) flow of Quantum Distortion Gravity (QDG), a metric-affine framework with gauged Weyl symmetry. We derive the classical foundations from first principles: the irreducible decomposition of the distortion tensor with an explicit inversion of the trace matrix, the Weyl-covariant distortion $\tilde D$, the no-go theorem for bare distortion invariants, and the Weyl-invariant ultraviolet action with distortion entering through $\phi^2 I_i[\tilde D]$. We then establish the constraint structure of the truncated theory (8 physical degrees of freedom, no spin-2 ghost) via a complete Dirac--Bergmann analysis, and analyze the BRST--BV quantization of the gauge algebra $Diff(\mathcal M) \ltimes Weyl$, including the antifield spectrum, the nilpotency proof, and the classical master equation. We compute the Weyl anomaly coefficients from heat-kernel data and prove the anomaly is cancellable by a Wess--Zumino term. In the main part of the paper we derive all one-loop beta functions from first principles, keeping every intermediate step. We show that in unitary gauge, the dilaton is a gauge mode and does not contribute; Proca fields contribute with three transverse polarizations and no Faddeev--Popov ghosts; Dirac fermions contribute via the Litim fermionic regulator. We extract the matter coefficients $a_S = +1/2$, $a_D = -2$, and $a_V = +3/2$ (the last for a Proca vector in unitary gauge), and we verify each by two independent routes. We derive the gravitational anomalous dimension from the explicit trace over TT graviton, trace mode, and Faddeev--Popov ghosts, reproducing the Litim result $A(\lambda)$ and $B(\lambda)$, and we display the ADM decomposition that yields the mode multiplicities. We show that the fixed-point equation $\beta_{\tilde G} = 0$ is genuinely quadratic in $\tilde G$ at fixed $\lambda$, we solve it explicitly, and we give the resulting discriminant. For the Standard Model matter content ($n_f = 3$, $n_V = 2$), we find a non-trivial UV fixed point at $\tilde G^* \approx 0.43$, $\lambda^* \approx -0.02$, with two relevant directions in the $(\tilde G, \lambda)$ sector, and we compute the stability matrix, critical exponents, and their numerical uncertainties. We verify robustness with a sensitivity scan, showing the fixed point exists for all $C_{\rm bl} > C_{\rm bl}^{\rm crit} \approx -1.02$, well above the QDG value $C_{\rm bl} = -3/(2\pi) \approx -0.477$; we give the analytic form of the critical line. We also analyze the heat kernel in a background field strength $F_{\mu\nu}$, showing that the mixing between graviton and Proca in the $(h^{01}, V^1)$ sector gives a negative contribution to the FRG coefficient $\hat c_V$ (distinct from the Weyl-anomaly coefficient $c^{\rm W}$), and we exhibit the second-order heat-kernel trace explicitly. Finally, we discuss scale generation via Coleman--Weinberg in a two-scalar extension, derive the flat-direction condition, and compare our results with the recent Proca--gravity fixed point of Pastor-Marcos et al. All symbolic and numerical calculations are performed in Python (SymPy, NumPy, SciPy), and the complete code is provided in the appendices, together with additional verification scripts.

items.summary: Reproducing a machine-learning result requires knowing how the experiment was run: the data, the model and its size, the optimiser, the learning rate, the batch size, the number of steps, the hardware and the seeds. This information is scattered through a paper---often only in a table caption or an appendix---and is increasingly extracted automatically by language-model pipelines, whose evaluations report how often they are right. We ask the two questions those evaluations leave open: when a pipeline is wrong, does it know it is wrong; and how much human effort does it take to find out? We build a benchmark of 80 arXiv machine-learning papers and annotate 24 of them (240 field decisions), 12 of them through two independent annotation passes, carrying verbatim, line-numbered evidence for every reported and every absent field; the passes agree on 97.5% of presence/absence decisions (Cohen's κ = 0.94), and the residual disagreements are adjudicated under a written scope rule. On that gold standard we run six extraction conditions of increasing agency---a single untruncated prompt, a tool-using agent, schema constraints, table/appendix re-reading, per-field self-assessment with a suspect flag, and mandatory evidence back-linking---over three difficulty strata, 432 full-paper extractions in total. Four results. First, agency buys no accuracy: present recall varies by one percentage point across all six conditions (0.883–0.894) while wall-clock time varies threefold. Second, honesty is a different quantity: 92% of the 387 wrong values were returned without any indication of doubt, and the share of returned values that are silently wrong falls from 12.7% to 5.5% only in the condition asked to flag its own doubts; requiring an evidence quote for every value restores the silent rate to 11.2% because it crowds out the doubt flag. Third, the errors are not inventions: every returned value that carries a checkable anchor occurs somewhere in the paper, and 375 of the 387 errors are values the document does contain—misattributions that belong to another configuration, another table, or the reference list, or values lifted from elsewhere in the paper—which is why a gold-standard-free anchor audit detects none of them (we report that as a negative result, with the five PDF text-layer artefacts it originally fired on pinned as a 22-case regression test). Fourth, human verification is the binding cost and it is predictable: verifying one field by hand requires a median of 12 candidate passages (up to 273; 4,707 in total for the gold sample) against one passage with an evidence link, although 4 of 25 spot-checked links failed adjudication, three of them because the quoted line does not hold the value. All corpus, prompts, gold annotations, adjudication records, raw runs, per-item API costs and analysis scripts are released with the paper, together with a per-session cost ledger ( runs/session-costs.json : the grid itself cost $2.84, the 644 sessions recorded in the released artefacts cost $3.22).

Given an arbitrary family of algebraic groups {Gi}r i=1 and elements Pi ∈ Gi with finite multiplicative orders oi = ord(Pi), we establish that the additive rank-coordinate space A(P) = Qri=1 Z/oiZ is canonically isomorphic to the external direct product of cyclic power orbits G(P) = Qri=1⟨Pi⟩ under the coordinate evaluation map ΦP(([ni]oi)i) = (Pnii)i. We prove that coordinatewise multiplication in the multiplicative state space corresponds strictly to coordinatewise addition of discrete expo- nent rank classes without introducing analytic logarithms, continuous curves, branch cuts, or topological ambiguities. We extend this framework to general category- theoretic limits, establishing that sub-space coordinate projections and factor permutation reindexings form natural transformations in the category of groups Grp. Finally, we formulate the extension to infinite complex power orbits , polynomial root reconstruction via Newton symmetrization of ranked power arrays Pr ∈ Cr×r, Chinese Remainder Theorem grid decompositions over composite moduli, native linear rank complexity bounds Θ(m), and an axiomatic minimal proof assistant kernel . items.summary: Algorithmic mathematical reasoning requires reliable decomposition, computation, and aggregation. Final-answer rewards provide limited guidance on intermediate errors, while successful execution does not guarantee mathematical correctness. This work proposes Function-Structured Graph Reinforcement Learning (FSG-RL), connecting subproblem graphs and Python implementations with multi-verifier feedback. The policy first learns to generate code from function graphs through supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) then optimizes the policy using answer-gated rewards and span-level credit assignment. The framework also supports teacher supervision and structured memory. A benchmark curated from Grade School Math 8K (GSM8K), MathQA, MATH, and Omni-MATH pairs public function graphs with private verification specifications. Under a unified evaluation protocol, GRPO improves final-answer accuracy from 43.25% to 67.50% and full solution success from 32.25% to 52.25% over SFT. Continued reinforcement learning (RL) with teacher supervision yields additional gains. The gains extend beyond producing correctly formatted code, supporting verifier-guided reinforcement learning for mathematical reasoning. Code is available at https://github.com/ZihanLiummyycc/FSG-RL.
items.title: Function-Structured Reinforcement Learning with Executable Verifiers for Mathematical Reasoning

items.summary: Abstract   The Universal Research System with Reverse Itinerary (SUII) is a retrospective analytical methodology designed to reconstruct, in a traceable and auditable manner, the probable pathway leading from an initial problem or question to a completed scientific product. This manual brings together the universal prompt, a mandatory common core, ten core modules—including bibliographic analysis (SUII-B)—and six specialised extensions: journalistic and opinion texts (SUII-P), audiovisual or audio documents (SUII-AV), legislation and regulatory documents (SUII-L), case law and judicial decisions (SUII-J), critical appraisal of scientific articles (SUII-LC), and traceable research information management for datasets and research data objects (SUII-TRIM). Each module guides the extraction of locatable traces, classification of the epistemic status of claims, and construction of matrices linking evidence, inference, confidence, alternatives, and required verification. SUII-TRIM extends this logic to the provenance, versioning, transformation, quality control, preservation, access, and reuse of research datasets, while preserving the distinction between directly observed information, information provided by the researcher, reasoned inference, and non-determinable information. The method separates retrospective reconstruction from the prospective generation of hypotheses and requires rival explanations whenever the evidence does not support a unique conclusion. It also incorporates procedures for methodological auditing, version comparison, conceptual genealogy, peer review, algorithmic-bias assessment, external validation, teaching, and traceable research data management. SUII is not intended to recover the authors’ actual psychological history or to replace validated tools for methodological appraisal, risk-of-bias assessment, certainty of evidence, data stewardship, or repository curation. Its application requires version-controlled corpora, decision logs, retention of prompts and outputs, source verification, preservation of original data objects when applicable, and mandatory human oversight. When the available traces are insufficient, the appropriate result is “not determinable.” The manual provides practical criteria for selecting, combining, and quality-controlling the modules according to the product under analysis and the research objective, while maintaining explicit boundaries between documented evidence, reasoned inference, speculation, and unresolved uncertainty .   Resumen   El Sistema Universal de Investigación con Itinerario Inverso (SUII) es una metodología de análisis retrospectivo orientada a reconstruir, de forma trazable y auditable, el itinerario probable que conduce desde un problema o pregunta inicial hasta un producto científico finalizado. Este manual reúne el prompt universal, un núcleo común obligatorio, diez módulos nucleares y seis extensiones especializadas: análisis bibliográfico (SUII-B), textos periodísticos y de opinión (SUII-P), documentos audiovisuales o sonoros (SUII-AV), legislación y normativa (SUII-L), jurisprudencia y sentencias (SUII-J), lectura crítica de artículos científicos (SUII-LC) y gestión trazable de información y datos de investigación (SUII-TRIM). items.summary: We present a complete, self-contained analysis of the one-loop functional renormalization group (FRG) flow of Quantum Distortion Gravity (QDG), a metric-affine framework with gauged Weyl symmetry. We derive the classical foundations from first principles: the irreducible decomposition of the distortion tensor with an explicit inversion of the trace matrix, the Weyl-covariant distortion $\tilde D$, the no-go theorem for bare distortion invariants, and the Weyl-invariant ultraviolet action with distortion entering through $\phi^2 I_i[\tilde D]$. We then establish the constraint structure of the truncated theory (8 physical degrees of freedom, no spin-2 ghost) via a complete Dirac--Bergmann analysis, and analyze the BRST--BV quantization of the gauge algebra $Diff(\mathcal M) \ltimes Weyl$, including the antifield spectrum, the nilpotency proof, and the classical master equation. We compute the Weyl anomaly coefficients from heat-kernel data and prove the anomaly is cancellable by a Wess--Zumino term. In the main part of the paper we derive all one-loop beta functions from first principles, keeping every intermediate step. We show that in unitary gauge, the dilaton is a gauge mode and does not contribute; Proca fields contribute with three transverse polarizations and no Faddeev--Popov ghosts; Dirac fermions contribute via the Litim fermionic regulator. We extract the matter coefficients $a_S = +1/2$, $a_D = -2$, and $a_V = +3/2$ (the last for a Proca vector in unitary gauge), and we verify each by two independent routes. We derive the gravitational anomalous dimension from the explicit trace over TT graviton, trace mode, and Faddeev--Popov ghosts, reproducing the Litim result $A(\lambda)$ and $B(\lambda)$, and we display the ADM decomposition that yields the mode multiplicities. We show that the fixed-point equation $\beta_{\tilde G} = 0$ is genuinely quadratic in $\tilde G$ at fixed $\lambda$, we solve it explicitly, and we give the resulting discriminant. For the Standard Model matter content ($n_f = 3$, $n_V = 2$), we find a non-trivial UV fixed point at $\tilde G^* \approx 0.43$, $\lambda^* \approx -0.02$, with two relevant directions in the $(\tilde G, \lambda)$ sector, and we compute the stability matrix, critical exponents, and their numerical uncertainties. We verify robustness with a sensitivity scan, showing the fixed point exists for all $C_{\rm bl} > C_{\rm bl}^{\rm crit} \approx -1.02$, well above the QDG value $C_{\rm bl} = -3/(2\pi) \approx -0.477$; we give the analytic form of the critical line. We also analyze the heat kernel in a background field strength $F_{\mu\nu}$, showing that the mixing between graviton and Proca in the $(h^{01}, V^1)$ sector gives a negative contribution to the FRG coefficient $\hat c_V$ (distinct from the Weyl-anomaly coefficient $c^{\rm W}$), and we exhibit the second-order heat-kernel trace explicitly. Finally, we discuss scale generation via Coleman--Weinberg in a two-scalar extension, derive the flat-direction condition, and compare our results with the recent Proca--gravity fixed point of Pastor-Marcos et al. All symbolic and numerical calculations are performed in Python (SymPy, NumPy, SciPy), and the complete code is provided in the appendices, together with additional verification scripts.

items.summary: Berggren's three matrices generate the tree of primitive Pythagorean triples and preserve the quadratic form x₁² + x₂² − x₃². Cha, Nguyen and Tauber (2018) built such trees for other integral ternary forms Q of signature (2,1). We ask whether the matrices alone determine Q. Main results: Recovery criterion (Theorem 3.1). A set of isometries of Q determines Q up to scale exactly when no nonzero vector is sent to plus or minus itself by all of them. Equivalently, the group they generate is not virtually abelian; for integral isometries, it acts irreducibly. The proof is elementary linear algebra and applies to arbitrary real groups. Berggren trees (Theorem 3.2, Proposition 3.3, Remark 3.5). Any two generators determine Q in Berggren's tree and in each of the five trees of Cha, Nguyen and Tauber. The definition of a Berggren tree alone does not force this: the generators A and A² give a Berggren forest for x₁² + x₂² − x₃² whose two generators both yield edges but do not determine Q. Roots at a rational null line (Theorem 3.6). For a primitive null vector P with divisor G, the minimum of Q on (P^⊥ ∩ ℤ³) \ ℤP is S = |det(2J)|/(2G²). An explicit congruence, Gm ≡ −τ (mod S), decides which minimal vectors e + mP are roots. N-cusps (Theorems 3.7–3.8, Corollary 3.9). For Q = ax₁² + bx₁x₂ + cx₂² − Nx₃² with D = b² − 4ac < 0, all data at the null vectors (p, q, 1) are explicit. A minimal root exists there if and only if gcd(G, S) divides D/G, and in particular whenever D is cube-free. Recovery by integral reflections (Theorem 3.12, Proposition 3.13). Minimal roots at two or three distinct rational null lines yield three integral reflections that determine Q. The paper also relates the reflections in the trees of Cha, Nguyen and Tauber to minimal roots (Remark 3.17), and states an open question for trees produced by their construction.

items.summary: Abstract We present a comprehensive, universal, abstract group-theoretic, module-theoretic, and category-theoretic formalization of bijectively separated rank arithmetic . Given an arbitrary family of algebraic groups {Gi}r i=1 and elements Pi ∈ Gi with finite multiplicative orders oi = ord(Pi), we establish that the additive rank-coordinate space A(P) = Qri=1 Z/oiZ is canonically isomorphic to the external direct product of cyclic power orbits G(P) = Qri=1⟨Pi⟩ under the coordinate evaluation map ΦP(([ni]oi)i) = (Pnii)i. We prove that coordinatewise multiplication in the multiplicative state space corresponds strictly to coordinatewise addition of discrete expo- nent rank classes without introducing analytic logarithms, continuous curves, branch cuts, or topological ambiguities. We extend this framework to general category- theoretic limits, establishing that sub-space coordinate projections and factor permutation reindexings form natural transformations in the category of groups Grp. Furthermore, when lane outputs collapse into a single target background group H, we isolate the exact relation subgroup KP =ker(ΨP) and prove the quotient isomorphism A(P)/KP∼= ⟨P1, . . . , Pr⟩ ≤ H, measuring the precise algebraic information lost during scalar collapse. Finally, we formulate the extension to infinite complex power orbits , polynomial root reconstruction via Newton symmetrization of ranked power arrays Pr ∈ Cr×r, Chinese Remainder Theorem grid decompositions over composite moduli, native linear rank complexity bounds Θ(m), and an axiomatic minimal proof assistant kernel . items.summary: We give an explicit convex polygon with 63 rational vertices whose area, after its shortest closed Euclidean billiard length is normalized to one, is smaller than that of Mallée’s parabolic triangle. This disproves Conjecture 2.2 of Balitskiy, Mitrofanov and Polyanskii (2026). The polygon was found by moving supporting lines near the parabolic triangle’s focal contacts and then discretizing the resulting shape. The proof checks the literal polygon in exact rational arithmetic: 63 width directions and all 39,711 triples of supporting edge lines. A three-file verification package contains the coordinates and an independent checker. The result identifies a better competitor, without claiming that it is optimal.
items.title: A rational polygonal counterexample to the Mallée parabolic triangle conjecture

items.summary: This repository supports research on single-channel speaker distance estimation : estimating the distance between a talker and a microphone from a single channel of reverberant speech. The record accompanies a series of papers investigating how reverberation, early and late room responses, and non-acoustic shortcut cues affect speaker-distance estimation. It combines a controlled synthetic corpus with real-corpus annotations and predefined evaluation splits. Source code and data-loading utilities are available at the project repository: https://github.com/michaelneri/audio-distance-estimation Dataset contents The record contains three main components: Synthetic RIR-variant corpus.  40,000 simulated speech clips arranged as 2,500 controlled acoustic scenes, with 16 paired variants per scene. Total size: approximately 25.9 GB. STARSS23 distance subset.  2,934 real speech clips extracted from STARSS23 and annotated with source–microphone distance. Total size: approximately 270 MB. Annotations and splits.  label tables, predefined folds, metadata, and reconstruction information for QMULTIMIT, VoiceHome-2, and the WHAM! noise conditions. These files contain no audio and are less than 2 MB. The downloadable archives are: synthetic_baseline.zip  10,000 clips with both propagation-delay and amplitude cues available. synthetic_gain_var.zip 10,000 clips with the amplitude cue disrupted by random ±6 dB source-gain variation. synthetic_onset_randomized.zip 10,000 clips with the propagation-delay cue disrupted by randomized onset padding. synthetic_both.zip 10,000 clips with both shortcut cues disrupted. shared_rir.zip 2,500 room impulse responses (RIRs) in .npz format, shared by all synthetic configurations. STARSS23_distance.zip 2,934 annotated real speech clips. labels_and_splits.zip   label tables, folds5.csv , and configuration metadata. They all use the same RIR collection and synthetic fold assignment. For each of 2,500 acoustic scenes , the dataset provides 16 paired signals . Room geometry, source and microphone positions, RIR, and speech segment are held fixed within a scene. items.summary: The Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB) is a neutral, derived research dataset for evaluating analytical methods under incomplete, conflicting, ambiguous, and reconstructable transactional evidence. OTEB is derived from the Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist . It provides a frozen reference cohort of 94,791 internally reconciled orders, 901 deterministic controlled instances, transaction-instance membership, evaluator-only oracle states, and state-specific monetary exposure. The benchmark represents four evidence states: `CONFIRMED`, `RECONSTRUCTED`, `CONFLICTING`, and `UNRESOLVED`. Controlled families cover missing evidence, hard conflicts, unique reconstruction, ambiguous reconstruction, duplicate evidence, and mixed corruption at 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40%. This release contains the reference oracle, controlled-instance definitions, compact membership index, exposure tables, data dictionary, provenance documentation, reconstruction code, validation code, manifests, schema catalog, and checksums. It contains no method predictions, comparative performance results, ablation studies, paper drafts, dashboards, or private Rahaskin data. Raw Olist CSV files are not redistributed and must be obtained from the original Kaggle source. Original source citation: Olist, & Sionek, A. (2018). items.summary: This repository provides the compiled analysis inputs, R code, figure source data and GIS rasters supporting the manuscript “Historical introduction pools pre-structure future plant invasion debt under climate change”. Version 2.0 contains the final USA-intersection climatic-analogue reconstruction and its corresponding model predictions and spatial summaries. The historical introduction pool contains 18,562 species. The stage-transition models use 5,791 complete-case species, of which 4,088 species without a recorded invasion form the future candidate invasion-debt subset. Future predictions cover 12 combinations of two climate scenarios (SSP126 and SSP585), three periods (2041–2060, 2061–2080 and 2081–2100), and two global climate models (HadGEM3-GC31-LL and MPI-ESM1-2-HR). The archive contains: • Figure_data: XLSX source workbooks for main Figures 1–4, Supplementary Figures S1–S4 and Supplementary Tables S1–S15, together with the compiled species-level analysis dataset and current and future candidate-species predictions. • Code: R scripts, computational inputs and provenance documentation for the stage-transition models, climatic-analogue searches, future predictions, phylogenetic null analysis, temporal analyses, sensitivity analyses and publication source tables. • GIS_rasters: GeoTIFFs for the main and supplementary spatial figures. Main Figure 4 rasters contain sums within globally aligned 0.5° display cells; supplementary spatial rasters retain the native 10-arc-minute resolution. • Validation: execution records and numerical checks. • README files: instructions for reproducing the analyses, plotting the source data and interpreting the spatial fields. Current and future closest US climatic analogue cells are identified separately for each candidate species. POT is the sum of future predicted invasion probabilities assigned to future analogue cells. CHG is future grid-level transition potential minus current grid-level transition potential, with unassigned cells completed with zero. CHG therefore incorporates both changes in predicted probability and relocation of climatic analogues. POSDP is the sum of positive species-level changes assigned to future analogue cells; Supplementary Figure S3 reports its range across the two climate models. The analytical workflow was tested with R 4.3.3. Reproduction starts from the compiled historical master dataset, supplied phylogenetic inputs, prepared species climatic centroids and extracted WorldClim grid values. The package does not independently repeat every upstream archive-curation decision, manual stage-status assignment, GBIF download or occurrence-cleaning step. These boundaries and the optional XLSX and GeoTIFF export procedures are documented in the README. The historical count of 15,950 candidate invasion-debt species is retained for historical summaries; it is not the population used for future predictions. This release supersedes the earlier spatial outputs based on a rectangular climate-search domain. Future results should be interpreted as conditional model projections rather than evidence of a statistically established climate-driven increase in invasion. The repository record is distributed under CC BY 4.0. The software license included in Code/LICENSE and the original terms of third-party inputs remain applicable.

items.summary: Controlling an agent with vision requires being able to separate useful information from irrelevant background information. JEPA-style latent world models seem like a natural approach for this, as they do not perform pixel-level reconstruction; however, they are still sensitive to these distractor signals and experience latent collapse. In this work, we introduce Controllability Factorized JEPA (CF-JEPA), a JEPA-style world model which splits the latent space into controllable and uncontrollable subspaces. This factorization allows us to capture all the distractor information into the uncontrollable region, while we use the control-relevant latent information for our task. With this, we show comparable performance across 2D and 3D control tasks under nominal conditions and improved performance under distracted conditions, where CF-JEPA is the only model that does not experience latent collapse. We also validate our model under distracted conditions for a simulated robot task, highlighting the practical application of such a scheme.
items.title: CF-JEPA: Improving Robustness of JEPA World Models via Controllability Factorization

items.summary: Recent video-based world models pair the scalability of autoregressive (AR) prediction with the visual quality of diffusion models. The choice of scene tokenizer is paramount for the optimal performance of each of these, both in terms of fidelity and semantics. Flexible-length, coarse-to-fine tokenizers yield exactly that: the first coarse tokens carry the clip's global semantics while later tokens further specify details. Existing flexible tokenizers only apply a representation-alignment (REPA) loss on early decoder hidden states, a target the decoder can partly meet from its noised input instead. We introduce SemanTok, a flexible video tokenizer that feeds frozen DINO features into its encoder and adds lightweight heads that reconstruct them from each retained token prefix alone. SemanTok achieves high semantic alignment and video fidelity at every AR model size: a 201M SemanTok AR model matches or beats a VideoFlexTok AR model $3.4\times$ its size, and larger SemanTok AR models further improve fidelity. It keeps semantic alignment on out-of-distribution classes and gives the decoder higher semantic alignment at every noise level, including pure noise. It performs well in both reconstruction and generation, and its short token prefixes are cheaper to predict and give better generation fidelity, with pixel detail deferred to later tokens.
items.title: SemanTok: Predictable Semantic Tokens for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation

items.summary: This chapter develops the research programme of Generative Relational Economics (GRE) by translating the conceptual, methodological, and substantive architectures developed earlier in the book into a cumulative, contestable, and revisable programme of inquiry. Its principal concern is answerability: GRE claims should specify what is being investigated, what kinds of evidence can support them, what would count against them, which methods are appropriate to their objects, and under what conditions their scope, formulation, or status should change. The chapter first distinguishes the epistemic status of GRE claims and establishes a modular research architecture. It then formulates research programmes for relational economic structures, allocation, heterogeneous value, value conversion and circulation, generative return, generative spacetime, fast–slow dynamics, economic power, justice, generative exploitation, epistemic economy, and AI-mediated capability asymmetry. These substantive programmes are complemented by domain studies, formal modelling, historical and interpretive inquiry, quantitative and empirical research, comparative theory, institutional experimentation, measurement analysis, counterevidence, negative results, replication, reinterpretation, and research infrastructure. A recurring concern is to prevent operationalization from collapsing the distinctions that motivate GRE. Measurement is therefore treated as a transformation with possible loss and reflexive effects; formalization is treated as task-relative rather than as evidence of ontological commitment; justice research keeps normative premises explicit; power and exploitation require mechanism-level identification rather than inference from asymmetry alone; and cross-domain translation preserves non-equivalence and domain-specific remainders. Failed models, failed translations, null results, counterexamples, and negative evidence are treated as constitutive resources for cumulative research rather than as residuals to be discarded. The chapter concludes by specifying how GRE may interact with neighboring Generative Relational domains while retaining disciplinary containment. Candidate cross-domain structures remain hypotheses for further inquiry rather than presumptive components of a completed general theory. GRE thereby emerges not as a closed theoretical system, but as an open research programme whose concepts, methods, models, and domain claims remain historically situated, empirically answerable, formally inspectable, and institutionally revisable.

items.summary: Reproducing a machine-learning result requires knowing how the experiment was run: the data, the model and its size, the optimiser, the learning rate, the batch size, the number of steps, the hardware and the seeds. This information is scattered through a paper---often only in a table caption or an appendix---and is increasingly extracted automatically by language-model pipelines, whose evaluations report how often they are right. We ask the two questions those evaluations leave open: when a pipeline is wrong, does it know it is wrong; and how much human effort does it take to find out? We build a benchmark of 80 arXiv machine-learning papers and annotate 24 of them (240 field decisions), 12 of them through two independent annotation passes, carrying verbatim, line-numbered evidence for every reported and every absent field; the passes agree on 97.5% of presence/absence decisions (Cohen's κ = 0.94), and the residual disagreements are adjudicated under a written scope rule. On that gold standard we run six extraction conditions of increasing agency---a single untruncated prompt, a tool-using agent, schema constraints, table/appendix re-reading, per-field self-assessment with a suspect flag, and mandatory evidence back-linking---over three difficulty strata, 432 full-paper extractions in total. Four results. First, agency buys no accuracy: present recall varies by one percentage point across all six conditions (0.883–0.894) while wall-clock time varies threefold. Second, honesty is a different quantity: 92% of the 387 wrong values were returned without any indication of doubt, and the share of returned values that are silently wrong falls from 12.7% to 5.5% only in the condition asked to flag its own doubts; requiring an evidence quote for every value restores the silent rate to 11.2% because it crowds out the doubt flag. Third, the errors are not inventions: every returned value that carries a checkable anchor occurs somewhere in the paper, and 375 of the 387 errors are values the document does contain—misattributions that belong to another configuration, another table, or the reference list, or values lifted from elsewhere in the paper—which is why a gold-standard-free anchor audit detects none of them (we report that as a negative result, with the five PDF text-layer artefacts it originally fired on pinned as a 22-case regression test). Fourth, human verification is the binding cost and it is predictable: verifying one field by hand requires a median of 12 candidate passages (up to 273; 4,707 in total for the gold sample) against one passage with an evidence link, although 4 of 25 spot-checked links failed adjudication, three of them because the quoted line does not hold the value. All corpus, prompts, gold annotations, adjudication records, raw runs, per-item API costs and analysis scripts are released with the paper, together with a per-session cost ledger ( runs/session-costs.json : the grid itself cost $2.84, the 644 sessions recorded in the released artefacts cost $3.22).

This disproves Conjecture 2.2 of Balitskiy, Mitrofanov and Polyanskii (2026). The polygon was found by moving supporting lines near the parabolic triangle’s focal contacts and then discretizing the resulting shape. The proof checks the literal polygon in exact rational arithmetic: 63 width directions and all 39,711 triples of supporting edge lines. A three-file verification package contains the coordinates and an independent checker. The result identifies a better competitor, without claiming that it is optimal.
items.title: A rational polygonal counterexample to the Mallée parabolic triangle conjecture

items.summary: Sunnycode v1 provides an open-access computational framework and reproducibility package supporting the research article Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization for Resilient Urban LoRaWAN Networks , submitted to Digital Communications and Networks. The framework integrates OpenStreetMap (OSM) building-level sensing demand, radio-frequency (RF) feasibility, capacity-aware gateway assignment, worst-case single-gateway failure retention (N−1), gateway-load fairness, and road-constrained Steiner backbone synthesis. The repository includes Python implementations of the proposed optimization approach and four independent benchmark methods (Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimization, Greedy, and Random Search). Dataset and experimental scope The computational experiment considers 685 building-level sensor anchors, 169 road vertices, 195 street edges, and 89 gateway candidates. The Full benchmark comprises 4,000 run-level observations obtained from 100 repetitions for each combination of five optimization methods and eight gateway budgets (k = 3–10). Repository contents Python source code and computational validation utilities. Nine original CSV files containing experimental observations, aggregated statistics, evaluation effort, and optimizer provenance. OpenStreetMap territorial input ( sunny3.osm ). Forty scientific figures in PDF format. Installation and execution instructions using Anaconda. SHA-256 file-integrity manifest and licensing information. The archived results support independent verification of the reported statistics and new computational experiments. The original historical environment metadata and detailed event histories are not included; therefore, bit-for-bit replay of the historical execution environment is not claimed. Scientific scope: RF coverage and packet delivery ratio are model-derived planning estimates rather than field-calibrated measurements. N−1 resilience represents gateway-access service retention and does not certify fault-tolerant physical-backbone connectivity. This software and dataset are released to support transparent computational research, independent assessment, and further development of resilient urban Internet of Things infrastructure planning.
items.title: Sunnycode v1 A Reproducible Framework for Failure-Aware Gateway Placement and Road-Constrained Backbone Optimization in Urban LoRaWAN Networks

items.summary: End-to-end research agents can now produce complete scientific papers, yet manuscript claims often diverge from executed experiments. This gap is structural: research state, failure histories, and claim-evidence alignment are not maintained as persistent, verifiable state across long-horizon pipelines. We present YouRA (Your Research Agent), an architecture for stateful, evidence-traceable autonomous research. YouRA preserves research state, execution evidence, and failure history across the research trajectory by integrating three components: a Verification State Architecture (VSA) that tracks hypotheses, gates, and evidence pointers; an Independent Controller that turns state and reflection records into lifecycle, recovery, and debate/review control while separating control from execution; and Stateful Reflection that logs failures as structured lessons and routes recovery through bounded repair, redesign, or reset. On MLR-Bench's predefined ten-task end-to-end subset, YouRA improves over both MLR-Agent and AI Scientist V2 on scalar Overall across all three matched backbones. An automated diagnostic using MLR-Bench's hallucination taxonomy reports intersection/union counts for four fact-based failure types, and data-provenance diagnostic shows more real-data-based outputs. Ablating each of the four components (the VSA, the Independent Controller, MCP tool access, and reflection-guided recovery) supports their separable contributions. Removing either core-state component drops YouRA below the full system. Code: https://github.com/PrayPrey/Your-Research-Agent.
items.title: YouRA: A Persistent-State Architecture for Evidence-Traceable Autonomous Research Agents

items.summary: Tackling complex real-world tasks can exceed the capabilities of a single large language model (LLM), motivating the use of multi-agent workflows that coordinate specialized agents to work together on these tasks. Recent methods train LLMs to construct better workflows from execution outcomes, but they optimize only the workflow generator, while the other agents that build or execute each workflow remain fixed even though every outcome depends on all of them. However, extending training beyond the generator is challenging: the agents are coupled, and a workflow's outcome is a single sparse score that cannot tell which agent causes a failure. We propose FloWright, which leverages the workflow as a harness to optimize workflows. By introducing a hierarchical, structure-aware reward paradigm, FloWright enables one role to self-evolve and two or more roles to co-evolve, with no additional models, labels, or executions. Considering the limitation that workflows are commonly trained and evaluated on data that a single agent can already handle, we further propose DataWright, an adaptive data hardening approach that converts existing datasets into workflow-level tasks with increased difficulty. Across document, slide, chart, code, math, and finance tasks, small open models trained with FloWright achieve improved performance by up to $+7.41\%$, with co-evolving ($+5.03\%$) more roles gaining more than optimizing one of them alone ($+2.83\%$). Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/FloWright/.
items.title: It Takes Workflows to Evolve Better Workflows

Not peer-reviewed.   Companion to HSH I (28 September 2026). Tier-2 material is not in this paper.     DISCIPLINE   HSH I derived a geometry and assumed a flux law. This paper keeps the geometry and splits the assumption. What is proved is proved about the toy model. What is not selected — a coupling, a bulk metric, a relativistic completion — is named and left open. Neural coupling and retrocausality are still excluded. They are not implied by anything below.     ABSTRACT   HSH I predicted a parabolic light curve by taking received flux proportional to the area of the brane slice. That step is not geometry. For a 4-ball translating along the hidden axis, orthographic area scales as ρ² and reproduces the parabola F₂ = 1 − (t/τ)². Uniform emission through the 3-volume of the same slice scales as ρ³ and produces F₃ = [1 − (t/τ)²]^(3/2). No uniform self-step weight puts the even sector on the five-value spectrum flagged in HSH I. Coupling remains the critical open problem. Ansätze are stated with kill criteria. items.summary: Resource limits are becoming an authorization boundary for AI agents that delegate work across concurrent and failure-prone workers. Parent-child allocation constraints, affine objects, and distributed escrow do not by themselves prevent overspend when replies are lost, effects complete after timeout, messages repeat, branches partition, or DAG joins alias one lineage. We formalize fault-tolerant budget conservation for distributed multi-agent delegation. Budgets are quantized resource vectors represented by exclusive escrow credits that move through a delegation DAG. Before dispatch, a branch converts credit into an operation reservation bound to lineage, epoch, normalized effect, maximum charge, receiver, and idempotency key. It persists a signed dispatch permit with quarantine; the gateway verifies that permit before first acceptance. Uncertain effects remain charged until authenticated settlement, a fenced authoritative no-effect proof, or permanent retirement. We prove ownership partition, ledger and effect conservation, descendant non-amplification, at-most-once settlement, late-completion safety, and partition confinement under explicit mediation, durability, authentication, normalization, and gateway assumptions. An indistinguishability result shows that partition-local availability requires exclusive preallocation. Bounded TLA+ checking, an independent JavaScript explorer, and crash-injected two-process SQLite experiments exercise the declared scope and detect timeout-refund and historical-certificate-validation mutants. The mechanism preserves the issued budget bound across the evaluated crash, retry, duplicate, partition, join, and late-completion schedules.
items.title: Fault-Tolerant Budget Conservation in Distributed Multi-Agent Delegation

items.summary: The Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB) is a neutral, derived research dataset for evaluating analytical methods under incomplete, conflicting, ambiguous, and reconstructable transactional evidence. The benchmark represents four evidence states: `CONFIRMED`, `RECONSTRUCTED`, `CONFLICTING`, and `UNRESOLVED`. Controlled families cover missing evidence, hard conflicts, unique reconstruction, ambiguous reconstruction, duplicate evidence, and mixed corruption at 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40%. items.summary: This repository supports research on single-channel speaker distance estimation : estimating the distance between a talker and a microphone from a single channel of reverberant speech. The record accompanies a series of papers investigating how reverberation, early and late room responses, and non-acoustic shortcut cues affect speaker-distance estimation. It combines a controlled synthetic corpus with real-corpus annotations and predefined evaluation splits. Source code and data-loading utilities are available at the project repository: https://github.com/michaelneri/audio-distance-estimation Dataset contents The record contains three main components: Synthetic RIR-variant corpus.  40,000 simulated speech clips arranged as 2,500 controlled acoustic scenes, with 16 paired variants per scene. Total size: approximately 25.9 GB. STARSS23 distance subset.  2,934 real speech clips extracted from STARSS23 and annotated with source–microphone distance. Total size: approximately 270 MB. Annotations and splits.  label tables, predefined folds, metadata, and reconstruction information for QMULTIMIT, VoiceHome-2, and the WHAM! noise conditions. These files contain no audio and are less than 2 MB. The downloadable archives are: synthetic_baseline.zip  10,000 clips with both propagation-delay and amplitude cues available. synthetic_gain_var.zip 10,000 clips with the amplitude cue disrupted by random ±6 dB source-gain variation. synthetic_onset_randomized.zip 10,000 clips with the propagation-delay cue disrupted by randomized onset padding. synthetic_both.zip 10,000 clips with both shortcut cues disrupted. shared_rir.zip 2,500 room impulse responses (RIRs) in .npz format, shared by all synthetic configurations. STARSS23_distance.zip 2,934 annotated real speech clips. labels_and_splits.zip   label tables, folds5.csv , and configuration metadata. MANIFEST.sha256 SHA-256 checksums for the downloadable archives. The four synthetic archives are independent and can be downloaded selectively. They all use the same RIR collection and synthetic fold assignment. Synthetic RIR-variant corpus The synthetic corpus is designed as a controlled experimental resource for isolating the contribution of different components of the room impulse response and two non-acoustic distance cues: propagation delay and received signal level. For each of 2,500 acoustic scenes , the dataset provides 16 paired signals . Room geometry, source and microphone positions, RIR, and speech segment are held fixed within a scene. Consequently, corresponding variants differ only in the specified experimental manipulation. RIR variants Each scene contains four acoustic variants: full — complete room impulse response. direct — direct path only, using a 2 ms window with a 5 ms half-cosine fade. no_early — direct path plus the late reverberant tail, with early reflections removed. no_late — direct path plus early reflections, with the late reverberant tail removed. The boundary between early and late reverberation is the room-specific mixing time , calculated from the mean free path rather than using a single fixed threshold. This allows the decomposition to follow the geometry of each simulated room. items.summary: This chapter develops the research programme of Generative Relational Economics (GRE) by translating the conceptual, methodological, and substantive architectures developed earlier in the book into a cumulative, contestable, and revisable programme of inquiry. Its principal concern is answerability: GRE claims should specify what is being investigated, what kinds of evidence can support them, what would count against them, which methods are appropriate to their objects, and under what conditions their scope, formulation, or status should change. The chapter first distinguishes the epistemic status of GRE claims and establishes a modular research architecture. It then formulates research programmes for relational economic structures, allocation, heterogeneous value, value conversion and circulation, generative return, generative spacetime, fast–slow dynamics, economic power, justice, generative exploitation, epistemic economy, and AI-mediated capability asymmetry. These substantive programmes are complemented by domain studies, formal modelling, historical and interpretive inquiry, quantitative and empirical research, comparative theory, institutional experimentation, measurement analysis, counterevidence, negative results, replication, reinterpretation, and research infrastructure. A recurring concern is to prevent operationalization from collapsing the distinctions that motivate GRE. Measurement is therefore treated as a transformation with possible loss and reflexive effects; formalization is treated as task-relative rather than as evidence of ontological commitment; justice research keeps normative premises explicit; power and exploitation require mechanism-level identification rather than inference from asymmetry alone; and cross-domain translation preserves non-equivalence and domain-specific remainders. Failed models, failed translations, null results, counterexamples, and negative evidence are treated as constitutive resources for cumulative research rather than as residuals to be discarded. The chapter concludes by specifying how GRE may interact with neighboring Generative Relational domains while retaining disciplinary containment. Candidate cross-domain structures remain hypotheses for further inquiry rather than presumptive components of a completed general theory. GRE thereby emerges not as a closed theoretical system, but as an open research programme whose concepts, methods, models, and domain claims remain historically situated, empirically answerable, formally inspectable, and institutionally revisable.
items.title: Generative Relational Economics - Chapter 22: Research Programme of Generative Relational Economics

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly construct multi-agent workflows that decompose a complex task and assign specialist agents from a pool. However, building such a workflow well remains challenging: how finely to divide the task, which agent to trust with each subtask, and when to create a new specialist are all critical decisions a workflow constructor needs to settle up front. Thus, whether each subtask succeeds remains unknown until the workflow runs. Yet, improving a workflow is costly. Locating a fault usually requires a reference answer, a graded outcome, or a trained assessor, and the fix is applied to the whole workflow through re-execution, re-search, or retraining. We propose InFlowOp, which prices every decision in one label-free cost that weighs how well an agent's competence meets what a subtask demands against how much that agent takes to run. Before execution, InFlowOp bidirectionally determines the granularity of task decomposition and agent assignment following from the cost rather than from a fixed template. During execution, InFlowOp corrects a fault with the cheapest move via the same cost that serves the workflow both as it is built and as it runs. Facing the workflow-level evaluation challenge, we introduce Braid, a benchmark whose tasks require multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent capability. Across various domains and backbones, InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to $+11.97\%$, achieving $+9.64\%$ with in-flow optimization. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/InFlowOp/.
items.title: Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: Label-Free In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization

items.summary: World models allow agents to plan in latent space by choosing a sequence of actions that most reduces the distance to a given goal state. Thus, planning can benefit from latent representations whose distances mirror commute-times in the environment. The spectral embedding space of the graph Laplacian provides such a representation, if it obeys a specific eigenvalue-dependent scaling. Unfortunately, instantiating the graph Laplacian is intractable in large, continuous environments. Self-supervised learning offers a natural route to such commute-time-preserving embeddings at scale. However, here we show that existing methods, which commonly encourage isotropic representations to prevent representational collapse, tend to degrade the "correct" eigenvalue-dependent scaling, leading to an inaccurate representation of commute times. To address this problem, we introduce Commute-Time-Preserving World Models (CTWMs), combining a latent displacement predictor and a log-determinant regularizer that prevents collapse, which provably recover the correctly scaled Laplacian representation under reversible deterministic dynamics and at the predictor's fixed point. In numerical simulations, CTWM matches or outperforms LeWM, a task-agnostic baseline, on several complex, continuous goal-reaching benchmarks, while using half the parameters.
items.title: Learning Commute-Time-Preserving World Models for Planning

items.summary: Code, partition manifests and per-image predictions supporting the audit and leakage-controlled re-evaluation of the 4,217-image Eye Disease Retinal Images collection.   Contents: the provenance and integrity audit; the manifests defining every evaluation arm image by image (image-level, patient-grouped, size-matched, source-matched, the common test set and the six leave-one-source-out splits); the training and evaluation code; stored per-image class probabilities for every run; the shortcut probes; and the visual adjudication verdicts for all 335 cross-label near-duplicate candidates.   The image collection itself is not redistributed here. It is available at https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/python16/eye-disease-retinal-images and the manifests reference it by relative path.
